analysis.one_liner: Blocks states from enforcing financial privacy protections stronger than federal law.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House Financial Services subcommittee at the end of the 108th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten two major financial laws so that states could no longer pass or enforce privacy rules for banks, credit bureaus, and other financial companies that go beyond the federal floor. It would also have made the existing federal preemption in the Fair Credit Reporting Act permanent. In practice, a bank in any state would answer to one national standard set in Washington, and state laws giving residents stronger privacy rights would be wiped out.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, credit card issuers, insurers, and credit reporting agencies gain a single, nationally uniform standard and are freed from a patchwork of stricter state privacy laws, lowering their compliance costs and letting them share and sell customer data under the weaker federal rules.

how_it_helps.text: It establishes one national privacy standard for financial institutions, replacing differing state rules with a single federal floor.
It removes the provision that lets state consumer protection laws providing greater protection than federal law escape federal preemption under the Fair Credit Reporting Act.

It bars states from imposing any requirement on consumer financial privacy topics already covered by the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, including how financial institutions disclose nonpublic personal information.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers bear the cost: they lose the ability of their state to set tougher privacy safeguards than federal law, and they keep only the federal rules, which at the time mainly required an opt-out notice rather than genuine consent before a financial institution shared personal information. State governments also lose regulatory authority over financial privacy.

drawbacks.text: The bill would strip states of the power to protect their residents' financial privacy beyond federal minimums, replacing stronger state protections with a single lower national standard.

Federal privacy rules under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act at the time relied on consumer opt-out rather than opt-in consent, so consumers in states with tougher laws would see their protections reduced to the federal floor.

The strongest good-faith argument for the bill was that a patchwork of 50 state privacy rules is costly and confusing for national financial firms; the honest cost of that uniformity is that everyone is held to the weakest common standard rather than the strongest.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real convenience for national financial companies — one set of rules instead of many — but its core effect was to take away stronger state privacy protections and lock in the weaker federal standard. For ordinary people, the cost outweighed the benefit: their financial data would be governed by the lowest common denominator, and states could no longer respond when federal rules fell short.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2003, sent to the House Financial Services Committee, and a few weeks later passed to a subcommittee, where it sat; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Patrick Tiberi introduced the bill on April 11, 2003, joined by Rep. Ken Lucas of Kentucky.
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services the same day.
On April 29, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit.
No further action was taken for the rest of the 108th Congress; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

The bill would have repealed the state override of preemption in the Fair Credit Reporting Act and established federal preemption over state consumer financial privacy laws under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and state governments came out ahead: because the bill died, states kept the power to enact financial privacy protections stronger than federal law, and banks and credit bureaus did not get the national preemption they sought. (Separately, Congress did make the Fair Credit Reporting Act's preemption permanent that year in a different bill, but the broader Gramm-Leach-Bliley privacy preemption in this bill was never enacted.)

for.name: Rep. Patrick Tiberi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to preempt state financial privacy and consumer protection laws.

for.name: Rep. Ken Lucas
for.what_they_did: Joined Tiberi in introducing the bill.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral — never scheduled a markup or vote
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit Subcommittee on April 29, 2003, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican — of the 8 members attached to the bill, 7 were Republicans and 1 (Rep. Lucas of Kentucky) was a Democrat — and no opposition ever recorded a vote because the bill never reached one.

industries.note: The bill would have freed banks, credit card issuers, and insurers from stricter state privacy rules and locked in the weaker federal opt-out regime, letting them share and sell customer data on the cheapest available terms. Consumers' financial privacy was the direct cost.

industries.industry: Credit reporting agencies and data brokers
industries.note: By repealing the state override in the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the bill would have prevented states from imposing stronger rules on how credit bureaus handle consumer data, keeping the federal floor as the ceiling.
States would lose the power to regulate consumer financial privacy and consumer credit protections beyond federal law, eliminating their role as a backstop when federal standards lag.
